content: The findings from various studies and meta-analyses on the effects of physical activity, including aerobic and progressive resistance exercise (PRE), on body composition, mental health, and functional capacity among individuals with high BMI or living with HIV are summarized below: 1. Body Composition and Exercise Interventions: Combined aerobic and PRE exercise, when paired with dietary or nutritional counseling, showed no clinically significant improvements in body composition compared to diet or counseling alone. However, the results were not deemed clinically important. Meta-analyses revealed no significant changes in body mass index (BMI), lean body mass, or fat mass for participants in PRE or combined PRE and aerobic exercise groups compared to non-exercising controls. Similarly, no differences were observed when these groups were compared to those receiving testosterone therapy alone. Waist circumference did not show significant changes in participants engaging in combined PRE and aerobic exercise compared to non-exercisers. However, there was a potential clinically important increase in limb girth among PRE participants compared to aerobic exercisers. Aerobic exercise was associated with reductions in body fat percentage, trunk fat, and limb fat, as well as increases in lean mass. However, the quality of evidence was limited due to methodological issues and small sample sizes. 2. Mental Health Outcomes: Aerobic exercise demonstrated clinically significant improvements in symptoms of depression and anxiety among individuals living with HIV. Participants in aerobic exercise interventions experienced reductions in depression-dejection scores compared to non-exercising controls. Resistance exercise and multimodal exercise interventions also showed positive effects on depression and anxiety, with significant reductions in symptoms observed in exercise groups compared to controls. However, the quality of evidence was affected by risks of bias and heterogeneity in study designs. 3. Functional Capacity and Fitness: Greater improvements were observed with high-intensity exercise compared to moderate-intensity exercise. Exercise time and strength outcomes also improved among participants in aerobic or combined aerobic and PRE groups compared to non-exercisers. Strength gains were more pronounced in PRE groups compared to aerobic exercise groups, with clinically meaningful increases in upper and lower body strength. Despite these findings, some outcomes, such as maximum heart rate and exercise time, did not reach thresholds for clinical importance. 4. Limitations and Bias: Many studies included in the reviews had serious risks of bias due to high withdrawal rates, lack of blinding, and inconsistent methodologies. These factors limited the generalizability of the findings. Heterogeneity in study designs, participant characteristics, and intervention types contributed to variability in results. Additionally, publication bias was suspected in some reviews. 5. Recommendations for Future Research: More high-quality studies are needed to validate the effects of different types of physical activity on body composition, mental health, and functional capacity, particularly in individuals with HIV-associated conditions or high BMI. In conclusion, while physical activity, particularly aerobic and resistance exercise, shows promise in improving mental health and functional capacity, its effects on body composition remain inconclusive. Further research is required to establish robust evidence and optimize exercise interventions for these populations.
